Layer 1 The United Kingdom, UK has introduced four mandatory conditions migrants must satisfy to qualify for permanent residency under its proposed earned settlement model, which will make obtaining indefinite leave to remain (ILR) dependent on applicants’ contributions and conduct.
Under the proposed reforms, migrants will no longer qualify for permanent residency almost automatically after five years in the country. Instead, the time required to secure settled status will depend on their earnings, contribution to society and immigration history.
The four non-negotiable conditions, which will apply to all applicants regardless of when they arrived in the UK, include:
1. Clean criminal record: Migrants must have a spotless criminal record, with the government proposing stricter requirements than the current rules, which allow some applicants with suspended sentences of up to 12 months to qualify.
2. High English proficiency: Applicants must demonstrate a high standard of spoken English, equivalent to A-Level English as a foreign language.
3. No outstanding government debts: Migrants must have cleared any debts owed to the UK government or taxpayer before qualifying for permanent residency.
4. Sustained National Insurance contributions: Applicants must provide evidence of sustained National Insurance contributions as proof of their economic contribution to the country.
Beyond these four mandatory requirements, the proposed model introduces different settlement timelines based on migrants’ earnings and contributions.
Under the arrangement, the highest earners could qualify for permanent residency after three years, while migrants earning more than £50,271 annually could become eligible after five years.
Certain public service workers, including doctors, nurses and teachers, would also qualify for settlement after five years.
Other migrants would be subject to a new standard settlement period of 10 years, while those who have breached immigration rules would have to wait at least 20 years before qualifying.
The government said the reforms recognise settled status as a significant privilege, granting migrants unrestricted access to the labour market, the National Health Service (NHS) and the welfare system.
The proposed changes are intended to make permanent residency a status migrants must earn rather than an entitlement granted after a fixed period.
